justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline trajectory for the asset, with prices expected to drift slightly higher over time from a near-term anchor around 154. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 154.1 is essentially a near-random-walk projection from the current price level, adjusted marginally upward by short-term momentum signals and the assumption that no major overnight catalysts will materialize. At the one-week horizon, the estimate rises to 154.8, reflecting a small positive drift consistent with the broader trend, while acknowledging that weekly noise can easily offset or amplify that drift. The one-month estimate of 156.5 represents a continuation of that gentle upward trend, implicitly assuming stable macro conditions and no significant fundamental repricing events during the period.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly ±3.9 points captures typical intraday-to-overnight volatility. By one week, the interval widens to roughly ±7.3 points, incorporating the possibility of scheduled data releases, central bank communications, or sector-specific news that could shift sentiment. At one month, the interval of roughly ±15.5 points reflects not just volatility compounding but also structural uncertainty about the macroeconomic environment, earnings revisions, and positioning dynamics that are genuinely difficult to forecast over a 30-day window.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include a sudden shift in Federal Reserve communication, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data such as employment or inflation prints, or a geopolitical shock that triggers broad risk-off repositioning. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings surprise or a dovish policy pivot could drive prices well above the upper bound of the monthly interval. Liquidity conditions also matter — thin markets can amplify moves in either direction in ways that historical volatility estimates do not fully capture.

It is worth noting that these intervals represent my probabilistic beliefs given available information, not hard boundaries. Tail events, by definition, fall outside stated confidence intervals roughly 10% of the time under ideal calibration, and real-world forecast error distributions tend to be fat-tailed, meaning genuine surprises occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest.
